title: Coral Islands of the Red Sea
summary: How tiny coral polyps build reefs, how reefs turn into islands like the Farasan Islands, why corals need sunlight and clean water, and how heat can harm them.
poll: Tiny animals can build something as big as an island.

versions.title: Islands Made by Tiny Animals
versions.text:
The Red Sea is by Saudi Arabia. The sea is warm. Coral reefs are in it.

A coral looks like a rock. But it is made of small animals! Each one is a polyp. It is soft. It is as small as a pea.

A polyp makes a hard cup. The cup keeps it safe. When it dies, the cup stays. New ones grow on top. So the reef grows. It takes a long time.

Small plants live in each polyp. They are algae. They use the sun to make food. They share it. They give the reef its bright hue. So the reef needs a clear sea and lots of sun.

Waves break bits off. Fish chew it. It all turns to sand. The sand heaps up on the reef. At last, it is a new island! Birds come. Plants grow.

Farasan has more than eighty islands. They are made of old coral rock. Sea turtles lay eggs there.

Lots of fish live on the reefs. Some live in no other place.

Hot seas can harm coral. The algae leave. The coral turns white. It may die. Keep the sea clean. Do not step on coral.

versions.title: Islands Made by Tiny Animals
versions.text:
The Red Sea is on the west side of Saudi Arabia. Its water is warm and clear. Under the waves are coral reefs.

A coral may look like a rock. But it is made of tiny animals! Each one is called a polyp. A polyp has a soft body. Most are as small as a pea.

Each polyp makes a hard cup. The cup is like a shell. It keeps the polyp safe. When a polyp dies, its cup stays. New polyps grow on top. Bit by bit, a reef grows. This takes a very long time.

Tiny plants called algae live in the polyps. They use the sun to make food. They share the food with the polyp. They give the coral its bright colors, too. So coral needs clear water and lots of sun.

Waves break off bits of coral. Some fish chew coral, too. The bits turn into sand. Sand piles up on the reef. At last, it sticks out of the sea. It is a new island! Birds land there. Plants grow.

The Farasan Islands are in the Red Sea. There are more than eighty of them. They are made of old coral rock. Sea turtles lay eggs on the sand.

Many kinds of fish live on the reefs. Some live in no other place.

Hot water can harm coral. The algae leave. The coral turns white. It may die. We must keep the sea clean. We must not step on coral.

versions.title: Coral Islands of the Red Sea
versions.text:
The Red Sea lies between Africa and Saudi Arabia. Its water is warm and clear. Under the waves are huge coral reefs.

A coral may look like a rock or a plant. But it is made of tiny animals! Each one is called a polyp. A polyp has a soft body and a ring of tiny arms. Most polyps are smaller than a pea.

Each polyp builds a hard cup around its body. The cup is made of a kind of stone. It keeps the soft polyp safe. When a polyp dies, its cup stays behind. New polyps grow on top. Slowly, the reef gets bigger. This can take thousands of years.

Tiny plants called algae live inside the polyps. They use sunlight to make food. They share it with the polyps. They also give coral its bright colors. That is why coral needs clear, shallow water with lots of sun.

Waves break off pieces of coral. Parrotfish bite coral and turn it into sand. Over time, sand and broken coral pile up on the reef. When the pile rises above the water, a new island is born! Birds rest there. Plants begin to grow.

The Farasan Islands are a group of more than eighty islands in the Red Sea. They are made mostly of old coral rock. Sea turtles nest on the beaches. Gazelles live on the land.

More than a thousand kinds of fish live on the reefs. Some live nowhere else.

Water that gets too hot can harm coral. The algae leave, and the coral turns white. If the heat lasts, the coral may die. We can help. We can keep the sea clean and never stand on coral.

versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and Saudi Arabia possesses an extensive coastline along its eastern edge. Its water is warm, salty, and exceptionally clear, and beneath the surface lie some of the most colorful and biologically diverse coral reefs on the planet.

A coral may resemble a rock or a plant, but it is actually a colony of tiny animals called polyps, each of which has a soft body and a ring of slender tentacles that capture particles of food drifting past. Most polyps are considerably smaller than a pea, although some form colonies that grow larger than a car.

Each polyp constructs a hard cup around itself, which functions like a miniature skeleton, and the cup consists of limestone, a mineral that the polyp manufactures from substances dissolved in seawater, and when a polyp dies, its skeleton remains as a foundation for subsequent generations, so the reef gradually expands, layer upon layer, over thousands of years.

Microscopic algae live inside the polyps in a mutually beneficial partnership called symbiosis, in which the algae use sunlight to manufacture food and share much of it with their hosts, while the polyps provide protective shelter in return. The algae also give coral its brilliant colors, which explains why coral flourishes in clear, shallow water that receives abundant sunlight.

Waves break off fragments of coral, while parrotfish bite the coral and grind it into fine sediment. Over many centuries, sand and broken coral accumulate on top of a reef, and when the pile eventually rises above the water, a new island forms, attracting birds and wind-blown seeds.

versions.title: Living Rock: The Coral Islands of the Red Sea
versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between the African continent and the Arabian Peninsula, and Saudi Arabia has a long coastline along its eastern shore, one lined in many places by living coral reefs that quietly build entire islands over the course of countless generations. Coral itself is not a rock but a colony of tiny animals called polyps, each with a soft body and a ring of tentacles used for feeding.

Each individual polyp secretes and builds a cup-shaped skeleton made of limestone, and as new generations of polyps grow directly atop the skeletons left behind by their predecessors, the reef gradually thickens and rises, layer upon layer, over thousands of years. Living inside the tissue of each polyp are microscopic algae, and together the coral and its algae form a close mutualistic symbiosis: the algae photosynthesize and share a portion of the food they produce with their coral host, while the coral in turn provides the algae with shelter and access to sunlight. These same algae are also responsible for giving coral much of its vivid natural coloration. This delicate partnership, however, depends entirely on clear, shallow, and consistently sunlit water to function properly.

Over time, the combined action of ocean waves and parrotfish, which bite and grind coral into fine sediment and sand as they feed, produces loose material that gradually accumulates until it rises above the waterline, forming an entirely new island. Birds and wind-carried seeds soon follow, gradually colonizing the fledgling landmass with life.

The Farasan Islands, an archipelago comprising more than eighty individual islands in the southern Red Sea, were formed in exactly this way, built from ancient coral rock accumulated over immense stretches of time. Today, sea turtles return to the islands' beaches to nest, while gazelles roam freely across the drier terrain. The surrounding Red Sea reefs support an extraordinary degree of biodiversity, hosting more than a thousand distinct species of fish, some of which exist nowhere else on Earth.

Unfortunately, coral reefs worldwide face a serious threat known as bleaching, a process in which heat-stressed coral expels the very algae it depends upon, turning a ghostly white and risking starvation and death if the stressful conditions persist for too long. Red Sea corals, however, appear to tolerate elevated temperatures somewhat better than many of their counterparts elsewhere in the world, a resilience that has drawn considerable scientific attention and ongoing study. Protecting this fragile, irreplaceable ecosystem requires simple but important actions: keeping the surrounding sea clean and free of pollution, and never standing directly on living coral, which can be damaged by even a single careless footstep.

versions.title: Living Rock: The Coral Islands of the Red Sea
versions.text:
The Red Sea stretches between the African continent and the Arabian Peninsula, and Saudi Arabia possesses an extensive coastline along its eastern shore, one lined in numerous places by flourishing living coral reefs that quietly construct entire islands over the uninterrupted course of countless successive generations. Coral itself is not, strictly speaking, a rock but rather a colony composed of tiny individual animals called polyps, each equipped with a soft, delicate body and an encircling ring of tentacles used primarily for feeding.

Each individual polyp secretes and gradually constructs a cup-shaped skeleton composed of limestone, and as successive generations of new polyps grow directly atop the skeletal remains left behind by their predecessors, the reef progressively thickens and rises, accumulating layer upon layer across many thousands of years. Residing within the living tissue of each polyp are microscopic algae, and together the coral and its resident algae form an intimate mutualistic symbiosis: the algae photosynthesize using available sunlight and share a substantial portion of the resulting food with their coral host, while the coral reciprocally provides the algae with physical shelter and reliable access to sunlight. These same resident algae are additionally responsible for imparting much of coral's vivid, characteristic natural coloration. This entire delicate partnership, however, depends absolutely on consistently clear, shallow, and well-lit water in order to function properly over extended periods.

Over extended spans of time, the combined erosive action of ocean waves and parrotfish, which bite and mechanically grind coral into fine sediment and sand particles as they feed, produces loose accumulated material that gradually builds up until it eventually rises above the surrounding waterline, forming an entirely new emergent island. Birds and wind-carried seeds subsequently arrive, progressively colonizing the fledgling landmass with increasingly diverse forms of life.

The Farasan Islands, an extensive archipelago comprising more than eighty individual islands situated in the southern Red Sea, were formed through precisely this gradual process, constructed from ancient coral rock accumulated across immense stretches of geological time. Today, sea turtles return faithfully to the islands' sandy beaches to nest, while gazelles roam freely across the comparatively drier interior terrain. The surrounding Red Sea reefs collectively support an extraordinary degree of biodiversity, hosting well over a thousand distinct species of fish, a number of which exist nowhere else on the entire planet.

Unfortunately, coral reefs across the world face a serious and escalating threat known as bleaching, a process in which heat-stressed coral expels the very algae upon which it fundamentally depends, turning a ghostly white and risking eventual starvation and death should the underlying stressful conditions persist for too extended a period. Red Sea corals, however, appear to tolerate elevated water temperatures somewhat more successfully than many of their counterparts found elsewhere around the globe, a notable resilience that has attracted considerable scientific attention and sustained ongoing research. Protecting this fragile and fundamentally irreplaceable ecosystem requires simple yet genuinely important actions: keeping the surrounding sea meaningfully clean and free of pollution, and never standing directly upon living coral, structures that can be irreversibly damaged by even a single careless footstep.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Tiny coral animals build reefs and islands in the Red Sea.
Sharks hunt fish all over the Red Sea.
The Red Sea is the biggest sea in the world.
People build new islands with sand.
questions.why: The article tells how polyps build reefs, how reefs can become islands, and how to keep coral safe.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about sharks.
wrong.C: The article does not say the Red Sea is the biggest.
wrong.D: The islands are made by coral, waves, and fish, not by people.

MID.prompt: Explain how living things and the ocean work together to build a coral island. Use at least three details from the article.

I explained how sand piles up to form an island.

MID.modelAnswer: Tiny animals called polyps build a coral reef by making hard limestone skeletons around their soft bodies, and new polyps keep growing on top of the old skeletons so the reef slowly rises over thousands of years. Algae living inside the polyps help give the coral its bright colors and share food made from sunlight, but if the water gets too hot, the coral can lose its algae in a process called bleaching. Meanwhile, waves and parrotfish break coral into sand, and that sand piles up on top of the reef until it finally rises above the water and forms an island.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why a coral reef depends on a partnership between two kinds of living things, and what happens when that partnership breaks down. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what the polyps and algae give each other.
I explained what happens during bleaching.
I supported my answer with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A coral reef depends on a close symbiosis between coral polyps and the algae living inside them: the algae use sunlight to make food and share it with the polyps, while the polyps provide the algae a safe place to live and build the hard limestone skeletons that form the reef itself. When ocean water becomes too hot, however, this partnership breaks down through a process called bleaching, in which the coral expels its algae and turns white, losing both its color and its main food source. If the heat lasts too long, the coral can die completely, which threatens the incredible biodiversity, like the more than a thousand kinds of fish, that depends on the reef and its sediment of broken coral and sand.
